chapters.title: Start here and study calendar
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). This front chapter carries no service and no exam-guide bullet. FREQUENCY's ranking of about 40 topics (section 1) and its 'hardest areas' (section 6: breadth of unfamiliar services, several workable answers, picking the MOST correct one) are the planning input for the study calendar: the reader's diagnostic was weakest in Design Secure Architectures (45%), so the calendar keeps the security-first order of LEARNING.md. FREQUENCY section 5 says SAA-C03 is still the current exam and that third-party claims of an 'SAA-C04' are contradicted by every official page. Registry note: the sources are the official exam page, the certification-prep page, the before-testing policy page (ESL +30 is requested before scheduling, Day 1 item), the exam guide landing page, its technologies-and-concepts page and the in-scope list; the certification FAQ is the faq source. Exam-policy facts are owned by chapter 01 (fact namespace exam).

chapters.title: How the exam asks, and exam English
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). This front chapter owns the fact namespace exam and carries no service and no exam-guide bullet. FREQUENCY section 4 lists the qualifier phrases that decide answers: 'LEAST operational overhead' and 'MOST operationally efficient' (reported as the most frequent qualifier; managed or serverless wins), 'MOST cost-effective' (cheapest option that still meets every constraint), 'MOST secure', 'highly available' vs 'fault tolerant', 'without downtime', 'minimize latency for global users', 'real-time' vs 'near real-time', 'decouple', 'privately', 'WORM', 'unpredictable', 'steady-state', 'can tolerate interruption', 'minimal code changes', 'temporary credentials', 'existing on-premises AD', 'static IPs', and '(Select TWO.)'. Stem pattern: 'A company... A solutions architect must... Which solution meets these requirements?'; a common technique is to read the constraint sentence (usually the last) first. 'No partial credit' for multiple-response items is a third-party claim only. FREQUENCY section 5: no new question types on SAA-C03 (ordering, matching and case-study items launched on other exams). Registry note: the exam guide root is the guide source (its index already exists); the policy pages before-testing, during-testing, after-testing, general-information (service short names shown by the in-exam Help button), recertification and benefits, the exam page and the certification FAQ carry the exam facts that chapter 01 must verify, among them exam-question-count, exam-duration, exam-passing-score and exam-esl-accommodation. The sample-questions PDF on d1.awsstatic.com is not recorded (binary; fetch it with --binary-to if the writer needs it).

chapters.title: The AWS map: global infrastructure, shared responsibility, Well-Architected
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Global infrastructure, the shared responsibility model and the Well-Architected Framework have no rank of their own in FREQUENCY; they appear inside other topics: 'Regions and Availability Zones' is an exam-guide bullet in four task statements (1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.2), 'highly available vs fault tolerant' (Multi-AZ) and 'MOST resilient / durable' (multi-Region, Direct Connect at two locations) are frequent qualifier phrases, and 'minimize latency for global users' points at edge locations (CloudFront, Global Accelerator). FREQUENCY section 1 row 41 lists Local Zones, Wavelength and Outposts as keyword recognition only (chapter 20 owns them). Registry notes: this front chapter teaches the general bullets about Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations and the shared responsibility model (1.1.K3, 1.1.K5, 2.2.K1, 3.2.K2, 3.3.K1, 4.2.K3) in addition to the service chapters that carry them (10, 13, 15, 16, 27, 28, 36). AWS CLI and AWS Management Console are recognition-only service cards (cards list); 'AWS CLI' is mapped to the key aws-cli here. The keys global-infrastructure and well-architected are not in the official in-scope list (registry warning R11 stays; a question cannot carry them). The Well-Architected Tool (chapter 38) shares the What's New tag aws-well-architected-tool with the Framework; the tool's case tag is used for the Framework. The global infrastructure page states no 'as of' date: cite counts as retrieved on the snapshot date. The general-information page holds the service short names that the in-exam Help button shows.

chapters.title: IAM
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). IAM is rank 3 of 42: 5 first-hand reports; very strong. Reported sub-topics: roles vs users, cross-account roles and trust policies, identity-based vs resource-based policies, reading policy JSON, SCP interplay, least privilege. Pairs to decide: IAM policy vs SCP vs permissions boundary (SCPs cap permissions and never grant them, chapter 04); identity-based vs resource-based policy for cross-account access (role in the resource account, trust policy naming the principal); roles and STS vs IAM user access keys ('temporary credentials always win'); IAM Identity Center vs Cognito (chapter 05). Stem signals: 'temporary credentials', 'MOST secure' (least privilege, temporary credentials), 'cross-account'. The reader's diagnostic domain Design Secure Architectures was 45%: this is the pilot chapter and the deepest in the identity part. Registry notes: the STS API reference is the second guide (no history or quotas page of its own; STS quotas are on the IAM quotas page). The key sts is mapped under the in-scope entry 'IAM' so that questions can carry it; side effect: the sts fact sheet is titled with the parent's official name. IAM has no pricing page (/iam/pricing/ redirects to /iam/; nothing is recorded). Bullet 1.1.S6 (federating a directory service with IAM roles) is shared with chapter 05, and 1.3.S4 (access policies for encryption keys) with chapter 06. Hands-on rule: no IAM users are created in tasks (RULINGS 2026-10-09).

chapters.title: Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower and RAM
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower and Identity Center are rank 25 of 42: 1 first-hand report plus exam-guide task 1.1; moderate. Reported sub-topics: SCPs cap permissions but do not grant them and do not apply to the management account; permission sets (chapter 05); Control Tower guardrails (now called controls). RAM appears in section 2 row 16 (sharing Transit Gateway or subnets across accounts) and in the Transit Gateway row 27. Pairs to decide: IAM policy vs SCP vs permissions boundary; consolidated billing and cost allocation tags belong to multi-account billing (bullet 4.1.K2 is shared with the cost chapter 41). Stem signals: 'multiple accounts', 'prevent any user in the account', 'landing zone', 'share with another account'. Registry notes: the Control Tower controls reference is a second Control Tower guide (no quotas page of its own). Organizations and RAM have no pricing page (both URLs return 404; the services are free); only Control Tower pricing is recorded. The What's New tag tag-policies is rare but belongs here.

chapters.title: IAM Identity Center, Directory Service and Cognito
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Cognito, federation and Directory Service are rank 35 of 42: no first-hand report; exam guide and syllabi; and section 2 row 7 lists Cognito, IAM Identity Center, Directory Service, STS federation and CloudHSM as reported gaps for tasks 1.1 and 1.2 ('app users vs workforce single sign-on; on-prem AD'). Pairs to decide: IAM Identity Center vs Cognito user pools vs identity pools (workforce SSO across accounts vs app sign-in vs temporary AWS credentials for app users); AD Connector vs Managed Microsoft AD vs Simple AD (proxy to on-premises AD vs real AD in AWS with trusts vs Samba-based). Stem signals: 'existing on-premises AD' (Identity Center with AD Connector or Managed AD), 'mobile app users sign in', 'temporary credentials'. Items that FREQUENCY says changed and must be checked in the guides: Simple AD is in maintenance since June 2026; AWS SSO was renamed IAM Identity Center (the old name may appear once as 'formerly'). Registry notes: IAM Identity Center has no pricing page (/iam/identity-center/pricing/ returns 404; the service is free). The Directory Service guide has three quotas pages (Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector, Simple AD); all are recorded. The What's New tag aws-single-sign-on holds the pre-rename items. Bullet 1.1.S6 is shared with chapter 03, 1.2.K5 with chapter 09, 1.2.S3 with chapters 07 and 08.

chapters.title: KMS and CloudHSM
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). KMS and encryption are rank 17 of 42: 1 first-hand report plus the official sample question on SSE-C; moderate to strong. Reported sub-topics: customer-managed vs AWS-managed keys, rotation, audit (CloudTrail), multi-Region keys; the four S3 encryption options (chapter 21). Pairs to decide: KMS vs CloudHSM (FREQUENCY says that since KMS reached FIPS 140-3 Level 3 the decider is single-tenant, customer-exclusive control or PKCS#11, not the FIPS level: third-party claim, verify in the guides before use); SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS with bucket keys vs SSE-C vs client-side ('keys kept on-premises' means SSE-C or client-side); customer-managed vs AWS-managed vs AWS-owned keys. Stem signals: 'MOST secure' (customer-managed keys), 'audit key usage', 'rotate', 'dedicated hardware', 'FIPS'. Registry notes: two prescriptive-guidance guides (KMS best practices, encryption best practices) are recorded as guides; their indexes exist. KMS has three quotas pages (overview, resource quotas, request quotas); all are recorded. Bullet 1.3.S4 is shared with chapter 03, 1.3.S7 with chapter 07 (certificate renewal), 1.3.S2 with chapter 21.

chapters.title: Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and ACM
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store is rank 30 of 42: 1 first-hand report; moderate; ACM sits in the WAF, Shield and ACM row (rank 29, 'certificates on ALB and CloudFront'). Reported sub-topics: automatic rotation, avoiding hard-coded credentials, Systems Manager Parameter Store (section 1 row 39: 'Session Manager vs bastion, Parameter Store, patching'). Pairs to decide: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store (native rotation means Secrets Manager); ACM public certificate vs imported certificate vs Private CA; where a certificate can be attached (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway; not directly on an EC2 instance). Stem signals: 'rotate automatically', 'hard-coded credentials', 'LEAST operational overhead' (Secrets Manager rotation), 'TLS termination', 'renew'. Registry notes: Parameter Store is a capability of Systems Manager (home chapter 38); the key parameter-store is mapped under the in-scope entry 'AWS Systems Manager' so that questions can carry it, and the Systems Manager user guide and its release history are recorded here too (the General Reference page carries the Systems Manager quotas; the guide has no quotas page). The Systems Manager FAQ page has only 7 questions. The What's New tag aws-private-certificate-authority is included for ACM Private CA items. Bullet 1.3.S3 (encrypting data in transit with ACM) is shared with chapters 14 and 15, 1.3.S7 with chapter 06, 2.1.K2 with chapters 25 and 31.

chapters.title: WAF, Shield, Firewall Manager and Network Firewall
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). WAF, Shield and ACM are rank 29 of 42: 1 first-hand report; moderate. Network Firewall and Firewall Manager sit in the security-detection row 37 (no first-hand report) and in section 2 row 6 ('which service inspects...'; third-party firewall appliances mean Gateway Load Balancer, chapter 14). Reported sub-topics: SQL injection and XSS rules, rate-based rules, Shield Advanced (response team and cost protection), central multi-account policy. Pairs to decide: WAF vs Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced vs Network Firewall vs Firewall Manager (Layer 7 rules vs DDoS vs VPC traffic inspection vs central policy); security group vs NACL vs Network Firewall for 'block an IP range' (chapter 10). Stem signals: 'SQL injection', 'cross-site scripting', 'DDoS', 'rate limit requests', 'across all accounts', 'inspect traffic leaving the VPC', 'domain filtering'. FREQUENCY section 5 says one vendor added Network Firewall and Security Hub recently (vendor emphasis, not proof). Registry notes: Shield and Firewall Manager are documented inside the WAF developer guide (one guide, one history page; their quotas pages are recorded separately). The DDoS resiliency whitepaper and the WAF implementation guidelines whitepaper are recorded as pages. Bullet 1.2.K3 (control ports, protocols and traffic) is shared with chapter 10, 1.2.S3 with chapters 05 and 07.

chapters.title: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Security Hub, Detective, Config and Artifact
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Security detection (GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Security Hub, Detective, Network Firewall, Firewall Manager) is rank 37 of 42: no first-hand report; the exam guide names GuardDuty and Macie; 'which service detects, scans or classifies' one-liners. Config is in row 28 with CloudWatch and CloudTrail (2 first-hand reports; Config rules, org trail). Pairs to decide: GuardDuty vs Macie vs Inspector vs Detective vs Security Hub vs Config (threats vs PII in S3 vs vulnerability scans vs investigation vs aggregated findings vs configuration compliance); CloudTrail vs CloudWatch vs Config (who called the API vs metrics and alarms vs configuration history and rules; chapter 37 owns CloudTrail and CloudWatch); Artifact for compliance reports. Stem signals: 'detect threats', 'find PII', 'vulnerabilities in EC2 and container images', 'track config changes', 'compliance report', 'single view of findings'. FREQUENCY section 5 says one vendor added Security Hub recently (vendor emphasis, not proof). Registry notes: seven guides, seven FAQ pages and seven history pages; Artifact has no quotas page and no pricing page (/artifact/pricing/ returns 404; the service is free). The Config FAQ is at /config/faqs/ (an older snapshot of /config/faq/ exists in the corpus and is not recorded). Bullet 1.2.K5 is shared with chapter 05, 1.3.K3 (data retention and classification) with chapter 21, 1.3.S1 (compliance) with chapter 06.

chapters.title: Amazon VPC
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). VPC core is rank 2 of 42: 5 first-hand reports and the official sample question on NAT; very strong. Reported sub-topics: subnets, route tables, internet gateway, NAT gateway (one per AZ vs shared), security groups vs network ACLs, bastion hosts (teach Session Manager instead, chapter 38), gateway vs interface endpoints. Pairs to decide: security group vs NACL (stateful, allow-only, ENI level vs stateless, allow and deny, subnet level; 'block an IP range' means NACL); NAT gateway vs NAT instance, one NAT gateway per AZ vs one shared (HA means one per AZ); NAT gateway vs gateway endpoint (private-subnet traffic to S3 or DynamoDB without NAT charges means a gateway endpoint); gateway vs interface vs Gateway Load Balancer endpoint (S3 and DynamoDB, free, route-table target vs ENI-based for most services, reachable from on-premises vs inline appliance inspection). Stem signals: 'privately', 'without traversing the internet', 'MOST cost-effective' (endpoint over NAT), 'highly available' (NAT per AZ), 'block traffic from a specific IP range'. FREQUENCY section 6 names NAT vs endpoint as one of the hardest pairs. Registry notes: this chapter owns VPC basics and introduces endpoints; chapter 11 owns peering, Transit Gateway, endpoints in depth and PrivateLink. The keys vpc-peering and vpc-endpoints (chapter 11) are mapped under the in-scope entry 'Amazon VPC' so that questions can carry them; side effect: their fact sheets carry the parent's official name. The What's New tag amazon-virtual-private-cloud is the older spelling of amazon-vpc; ipv6-at-aws is included for IPv6 items. Bullet 1.1.K3 (Regions and AZs) is also in chapter 02; 4.4.S3 (routes that minimize transfer costs, VPC endpoints) is shared with chapters 11 and 15.

chapters.title: Connecting VPCs: peering, Transit Gateway, endpoints and PrivateLink
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Transit Gateway, peering, PrivateLink and endpoints are rank 27 of 42: 2 first-hand reports; moderate. Reported sub-topics: transitive routing, segmentation, PrivateLink, RAM sharing of a Transit Gateway (chapter 04). Pairs to decide: peering vs Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink (few VPCs and non-transitive vs hub-and-spoke at scale with transitive routing vs exposing one service to many consumers, overlapping CIDRs allowed); gateway vs interface vs Gateway Load Balancer endpoint (chapter 10 introduces them); endpoint vs NAT gateway for cost. Stem signals: 'privately', 'without traversing the internet', 'hundreds of VPCs', 'overlapping CIDR', 'expose a service to other accounts', 'reduce data transfer charges'. Registry notes: peering has no What's New tag and no case tag of its own (its items carry amazon-vpc; its change feed holds the document-history rows only); the VPC FAQ holds the peering questions, so it is recorded here as well. The key vpc-endpoints has no separate guide: the PrivateLink guide documents endpoints, and its history and quotas pages serve both keys. Bullet 4.4.S3 is shared with chapters 10 and 15, 3.4.K4 and 3.4.S1 with chapter 12, 4.4.S5 (reviewing workloads for network optimizations) is a review bullet placed here because endpoint and Transit Gateway charges are its usual subject.

chapters.title: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect and Client VPN
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Hybrid connectivity (Direct Connect, VPN) is rank 26 of 42: 2 first-hand reports; moderate. Reported sub-topics: Direct Connect vs VPN provisioning time and performance, VPN over Direct Connect for encryption, Direct Connect resilience (two locations), bandwidth choice. Pairs to decide: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect (fast and encrypted over the internet vs consistent private bandwidth with weeks of lead time; encryption on Direct Connect means VPN over Direct Connect; Direct Connect backup means VPN; maximum resilience means two Direct Connect locations); Client VPN vs Site-to-Site VPN (individual users vs network to network; the current in-scope list names them separately). Stem signals: 'consistent network performance', 'dedicated connection', 'within days', 'encrypt traffic over Direct Connect', 'remote employees', 'MOST resilient'. Registry notes: the Direct Connect document-history page is named AboutThisGuide.html (its title is 'Document history'); it is recorded as the history page. The Direct Connect pricing address /directconnect/pricing/ redirects to /directconnect/pricing/pay-as-you-go/, which is recorded (the redirecting snapshot stays in the corpus and is in no list). The VPN FAQ page covers both Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN. The What's New tag aws-site-to-site is the Site-to-Site VPN tag; aws-vpn holds older items. Bullets 3.4.K4 and 3.4.S1 are shared with chapter 11.

chapters.title: Amazon Route 53
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Route 53 is rank 19 of 42: 1 first-hand report and recurring in student feedback; moderate to strong. Reported sub-topics: all routing policies, health checks, alias vs CNAME, private hosted zones. Pairs to decide: latency vs geolocation vs geoproximity routing (best performance vs user location for compliance or localisation vs resource-location bias), weighted for canary releases, failover for active-passive, multivalue answer; alias vs CNAME (zone apex and AWS targets mean alias); ELB vs Route 53 vs EC2 health checks (DNS failover means Route 53). Stem signals: 'route users to the nearest Region', 'users in a specific country', 'zone apex', 'DNS failover', 'resolve on-premises names'. Registry notes: 'Amazon Route 53' is mapped to the key route53 here. The guide's automatic quotas pointer picked the load-balancer quotas page; the recorded quotas page is DNSLimitations (title 'Quotas'). The history page is History.html. Application Recovery Controller is documented in the Route 53 guide family but is not in the in-scope list. Bullet 2.2.K1 (Regions, AZs, Route 53) is also in chapter 02; 2.2.K6 (failover strategies) and 2.2.S2 are shared with the HA and DR chapter 40.

chapters.title: Elastic Load Balancing
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). ELB is rank 10 of 42: 3 first-hand reports; strong. Reported sub-topics: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB (an exam-guide skill), health checks, sticky sessions, TLS offload. Pairs to decide: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB (Layer 7 path and host routing, WAF, Lambda targets vs Layer 4 TCP and UDP, static IPs, extreme performance vs third-party appliances); 'static IP required' means NLB with Elastic IPs or Global Accelerator (ALB has none); ELB vs Route 53 vs EC2 health checks (an Auto Scaling group should use the ELB health check type for application-level health). Stem signals: 'static IP', 'allow-list', 'millions of requests per second', 'path-based routing', 'third-party firewall appliances', 'TLS termination'. Registry notes: four guides (the general user guide plus one per load balancer type); the general guide has no history or quotas page, the three type guides have both. Classic Load Balancer is documented separately and is not taught as an answer. Bullet 1.3.S3 (TLS with ACM) is shared with chapters 07 and 15; 2.1.K10 (multi-tier architectures) with the patterns chapters; 2.2.S4 (single points of failure) with chapter 10.

chapters.title: CloudFront and Global Accelerator
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). CloudFront is rank 14 of 42: 2 first-hand reports and reported as a recurring exam topic in student feedback; strong. Global Accelerator is rank 22: 1 first-hand report that names CloudFront vs Global Accelerator as a hardest comparison, plus exam-guide examples; moderate. Reported sub-topics: latency scenarios, path-based behaviors, Lambda@Edge, origin access control (OAI is legacy), signed URLs and cookies; static anycast IPs, TCP and UDP, Regional failover. Pairs to decide: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator (HTTP caching at the edge vs TCP and UDP with two static anycast IPs, fast failover and no caching); S3 presigned URL vs CloudFront signed URL vs signed cookies vs OAC ('bucket only via CloudFront' means OAC); Lambda@Edge vs CloudFront Functions (heavier logic or network calls vs lightweight header and URL rewrites; CloudFront Functions is FREQUENCY's own addition); S3 Transfer Acceleration vs CloudFront vs multipart upload (chapter 21). Stem signals: 'minimize latency for global users', 'static IPs' or 'allow-list', 'non-HTTP traffic', 'restrict access to the bucket', 'edge caching'. Registry notes: CloudFront has a second quotas page for SSL/TLS certificates (recorded). The ddos whitepaper and the fault-isolation appendix on edge network services are recorded for the 'edge locations' part of bullet 3.2.K2, which is also in chapter 02. Bullet 1.3.S3 (TLS with ACM on CloudFront) is shared with chapters 07 and 14; 4.4.S3 with chapters 10 and 11.

chapters.title: Amazon EC2
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). EC2 and purchasing options are rank 4 of 42: 4 first-hand reports and 4 of the 10 official sample questions; strong. Reported sub-topics: On-Demand vs Reserved Instances vs Spot, hibernation, failover with a secondary network interface, instance families, placement groups, instance store (chapter 22). Official sample questions: hibernation to keep in-memory state; a secondary network interface for failover; On-Demand instead of Spot for jobs that must not be interrupted. Pairs to decide: On-Demand vs Reserved Instances or Savings Plans vs Spot vs Dedicated Hosts vs Capacity Reservations; placement groups cluster vs spread vs partition; hibernate vs stop vs instance store; Lambda vs Fargate vs ECS on EC2 vs EC2 vs Batch. Stem signals: 'can tolerate interruption' (Spot), 'steady-state' or '1 to 3 years' (Reserved Instances or Savings Plans), 'MOST cost-effective' (the cheapest option that still meets every constraint), licences bound to sockets or cores (Dedicated Hosts). Savings Plans types and Database Savings Plans belong to chapter 41. FREQUENCY lists a Graviton emphasis as an unverified claim of vendor sites. Registry notes: the in-scope entry Amazon EC2 is mapped to the keys ec2 and instance-store (chapter 22), so that questions can carry the key instance-store; bullet 4.2.K3 (Regions and Availability Zones in the compute cost task) lives here because chapter 02 has no questions.

chapters.title: EC2 Auto Scaling
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). EC2 Auto Scaling is rank 11 of 42: 2 first-hand reports and 2 of the 10 official sample questions; strong. Reported sub-topics: target tracking, step scaling with instance warm-up, scheduled actions, ELB health checks, lifecycle hooks, groups across several Availability Zones. Official sample questions: step scaling with warm-up; new subnets in a new Availability Zone plus Auto Scaling group, ALB and RDS Multi-AZ (Select TWO). Pairs to decide: target tracking vs step vs scheduled vs predictive scaling; ELB health check vs EC2 health check for the group; horizontal vs vertical scaling. Stem signals: 'decouple', 'cannot keep up', 'spikes' (scale workers on queue depth, with chapter 31); 'highly available' (a group across Availability Zones behind a load balancer). AWS Auto Scaling (scaling plans) and Application Auto Scaling appear in no first-hand report; the exam guide names AWS Auto Scaling in bullet 3.2.K4, so a recognition-level service card is enough (registry key aws-auto-scaling is in the cards list). Registry notes: the What's New tag auto-scaling is generic and also holds Application Auto Scaling and ECS items; its items were harvested into both change feeds.

chapters.title: AWS Lambda
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Lambda and serverless are rank 6 of 42: 4 first-hand reports; strong. Reported sub-topics: limits and memory sizing (also named in the exam guide), triggers, SQS to Lambda, function URLs (one 2023 report), Lambda@Edge (chapter 15), pairing with RDS Proxy (chapter 26). Pairs to decide: Lambda vs Fargate vs ECS on EC2 vs EC2 vs Batch; Step Functions vs SQS vs chained Lambda functions (chapter 32). Stem signals: 'LEAST operational overhead' (managed or serverless), 'unpredictable' or 'spiky' traffic, 'event-driven', 'runs for a few seconds on each upload'. Value that FREQUENCY says changed and that must be checked in the guide before use: the maximum run time of a function. Older material assumes one fixed limit; FREQUENCY reports a longer limit for asynchronous invocations on Lambda Managed Instances, announced in September 2026. That is after the exam eligibility cutoff, so label it not examinable yet. Source note: the guide has a second quotas page for Lambda Managed Instances; the main quotas page is gettingstarted-limits.

chapters.title: ECS, EKS, Fargate and ECR
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Containers (ECS, EKS, Fargate, ECR) are rank 5 of 42: 5 first-hand reports, and one says 'more than expected'; strong. Reported sub-topics: Fargate vs EC2 launch type, task roles, ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere, EKS Cluster Autoscaler and Metrics Server, Karpenter, migrating applications to containers. FREQUENCY suggests more depth than a typical medium chapter, mainly for EKS scaling. Pairs to decide: ECS vs EKS (existing Kubernetes, portability, EKS Anywhere vs the simplest AWS-native choice); Fargate vs Lambda; Fargate vs EC2 capacity. Stem signals: 'LEAST operational overhead' (Fargate), 'existing Kubernetes', 'minimal code changes'. Registry notes: ECS Anywhere, EKS Anywhere and EKS Distro are recognition-only service cards (cards list). EKS Anywhere and EKS Distro have no guide on an allowed host, so use their product and FAQ pages and the EKS deployment options page. What's New has no tag for the two Anywhere products; their items carry amazon-ecs and amazon-eks. AWS App Runner appears in the decision guides and in the Containers on AWS whitepaper, but it is not in the in-scope list and it is on the Services in Maintenance page: do not teach it as an answer. App2Container is the AWS tool behind bullet 2.1.K8; it is not an in-scope entry.

chapters.title: More compute: Beanstalk, Batch, Outposts, Local Zones, Wavelength
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Edge and HPC compute (Outposts, Local Zones, Wavelength, Batch) is rank 41 of 42: no first-hand report; exam guide and syllabi only; keyword recognition. Elastic Beanstalk (with CloudFormation) is rank 33: 2 first-hand reports; moderate to weak; 'least-ops deployment'. Reported use: edge, data residency and low latency (Outposts, Local Zones, Wavelength); long batch jobs and HPC (Batch). Pairs to decide: Beanstalk vs CloudFormation (chapter 38); Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2 vs Batch; Outposts vs Local Zones vs Wavelength. VMware Cloud on AWS and the Serverless Application Repository are not mentioned in FREQUENCY: recognition only. Registry notes: Local Zones is a chapter key but not an entry of the official in-scope list (registry check warning R11 stays; a question cannot carry the key local-zones). The AWS page for VMware Cloud on AWS opens with a notice about who sells the service since April 30, 2024: read the snapshot before writing the card. The address /vmware/faqs/ redirects to that product page, which holds the questions. VMware documentation is not on an allowed host. chapters.title: Amazon S3
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). S3 is rank 1 of 42: 6 first-hand reports, 2 of the 10 official sample questions, all syllabi; very strong. Reported sub-topics: storage classes and minimum storage durations, lifecycle rules, Intelligent-Tiering, versioning, replication (CRR and SRR), Object Lock, encryption options (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side), presigned URLs, CORS, access points, event notifications, Transfer Acceleration, multipart upload, Requester Pays. Official sample questions: CORS; SSE-C or client-side encryption when keys stay on premises. Pairs to decide: the storage classes; Object Lock compliance vs governance mode vs versioning with MFA delete; the four encryption options; presigned URL vs CloudFront signed URL or cookies vs origin access control (chapter 15); Transfer Acceleration vs CloudFront vs multipart upload; S3 vs EBS vs EFS. Stem signals: 'WORM', 'cannot be deleted or modified', 'unknown access pattern', 'MOST cost-effective'. Items that FREQUENCY says changed and that must be checked in the guides before use: the maximum object size (older material: 5 TB); S3 Select, S3 Glacier Select and S3 Object Lambda are on the Services in Maintenance page (Athena is the SQL-on-S3 answer); the Glacier vault API is in maintenance, the Glacier storage classes are not; small objects in Intelligent-Tiering are not auto-tiered. Registry note: this chapter has 18 bullets; five of them are in the security task 1.3, the reader's weakest domain.

Stem signals: 'highest IOPS', 'sustained IOPS', 'throughput-intensive sequential', 'cold data', 'temporary data', 'boot volume'. The exam guide names block storage options (HDD and SSD volume types) in bullet 4.1.K6 and Provisioned IOPS in bullet 3.3.K4 (chapter 26). Registry notes: instance store is documented in the EC2 User Guide, so that guide is also a guide of this chapter and the instance store pages are in sources.pages; the key instance-store is mapped to the in-scope entry Amazon EC2. The What's New feed and the document history of the EC2 guide are harvested under the service name ec2.

chapters.title: Cost optimization
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Cost tools are rank 40 of 42: 1 first-hand report (generic), but the exam guide repeats the same two knowledge bullets (cost management service features; cost management tools) in every Domain 4 task, so 8 bullets here share two texts. Reported sub-topics: the four cost services, cost allocation tags, Savings Plans types, Compute Optimizer and Trusted Advisor (chapter 38). Purchasing options are part of rank 4 (EC2). Task 4.4 (cost-optimized network architectures) is taught here as the network-cost half of the chapter: NAT gateway vs NAT instance, one shared NAT gateway vs one per AZ (4.4.K4, 4.4.S1); Direct Connect vs VPN vs internet and bandwidth (4.4.K5, 4.4.S2, 4.4.S7); Transit Gateway vs VPC peering, data-transfer routes between AZs, Regions and the internet, gateway endpoints (4.4.K6, 4.4.S3); load balancer and DNS cost dimensions (4.4.K3, 4.4.K7). The network facts live in the canon of chapters 10 to 15; this chapter adds the pricing dimensions (the network pricing pages are in sources.pricing for that reason). Pairs to decide: Cost Explorer vs Budgets vs Cost and Usage Report vs Compute Optimizer vs Trusted Advisor; Compute vs EC2 Instance Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances; On-Demand vs Reserved or Savings Plans vs Spot vs Dedicated Host vs Capacity Reservation (chapter 16); NAT gateway vs gateway endpoint (a reported hardest pair). Stem signals: 'MOST cost-effective' means the cheapest option that still meets every constraint; 'steady-state' or '1 to 3 years'; 'can tolerate interruption'. FREQUENCY names Database Savings Plans as new in December 2025; check it in the Savings Plans guide before use. Level: the four cost services are service cards inside this pattern chapter. Source notes: Savings Plans has no What's New tag (cloud-financial-management is used); the Cost and Usage Report is in the AWS Data Exports User Guide.

chapters.title: Security patterns
chapters.notes: Frequency note (third-party research from _build/spec/FREQUENCY.md; planning input only, never evidence). Security is not one ranked topic; it is spread over IAM (rank 3), KMS and encryption (rank 17), Organizations and SCPs (rank 25), WAF, Shield and ACM (rank 29), Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store (rank 30), Cognito and federation (rank 35) and the detection services (rank 37). Section 6 lists security depth (IAM policy logic, cross-account access, SCPs, KMS) as a main reason for failing; one report calls security the hardest area. The reader's diagnostic result for Domain 1 was 45% (READER.md), so this pattern chapter is the repair chapter for her weakest domain.
